full_text:
Baker Mayfield and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers are favored to beat out reigning NFC South champions Bryce Young and the Carolina Panthers for the division crown in 2026. Julio Aguilar / Getty Images
Single-digit wins have been enough to claim the NFC South crown in three of the past four seasons — and it’ll likely be enough to do it again in 2026.
The Athletic ‘s predictive analyst Austin Mock forecasts all four teams to finish with between six and eight wins while sportsbooks like DraftKings list odds that give each between an 18 and 35 percent implied probability to come out on top. Let’s take a look at the board, then dive into Mock’s projections and his take on what will be the tightest (if weakest) division race of the NFL season.
The NFC South is such a toss up — no team stands head and shoulders above the rest, which means all four are capable of winning the division.
I mostly agree that the Bucs should be considered the favorites going into the season. They have arguably the best quarterback in the division, maybe even the best overall roster. But at this point, am I trusting them without longtime stars Mike Evans and Lavonte David? How do they replace those guys? There is some serious uncertainty there.
I’m not sure I’m a believer in the Panthers just yet given their uncertainty at offensive tackle, but they are still capable of winning this division about one-fifth of the time.
I was quite excited about the Saints and their offense under head coach Kellen Moore this time last month, but it doesn’t look like first-round rookie wide receiver Jordyn Tyson will be ready anytime soon.
Meanwhile, the Falcons have yet to pick a Week 1 starter from their crowded quarterback room .
I’m not very confident in any of these teams, so calling this the tightest division in the NFL is pretty spot on — even if it’s because it’s the worst in football.
Last season, the Panthers claimed the crown after winning only eight games by emerging from a three-way tiebreaker. This season, I firmly believe eight wins could once again be enough for any of these teams to take the title. My model believes every NFC South team is a below-average NFL team, all sitting within two points of each other from a power rating perspective.

After ranking NFC teams 1-16 on Wednesday , six NFL team executives are back to stack the AFC as the 2026 regular season approaches.

full_text:
Josh Allen enters his first NFL season without Sean McDermott as his head coach, as Joe Brady takes over. Jason Miller / Getty Images
After ranking NFC teams 1-16 on Wednesday , six NFL team executives are back to stack the AFC as the 2026 regular season approaches.
Is this finally the Buffalo Bills’ year? Four of the six execs have Buffalo at the top. In a change, the Chiefs failed to crack the top five. Are they too low?
We answer those questions and more in a run-through of all 16 teams, from Buffalo to Miami, ranked below in median order, with average as a tiebreaker.
Votes: 2-1-1-1-2-1 | Avg: 1.3 | Median: 1 | Vegas wins: 10.5 (T-2nd-AFC)
Tier votes: SB contender: 6
The Bills top the AFC this year almost by default amid perceptions that Kansas City and Baltimore have regressed, while Denver and New England remain a tick behind.
"Josh Allen is the best player in the league," one exec said.
While some criticized the price Buffalo paid in the offseason when acquiring DJ Moore from Chicago, one of the execs in this survey said he expected big things from the receiver in Buffalo.
"My hardest choice was Houston-Buffalo (for the top spot)," another exec said. "The defensive change (under new coordinator Jim Leonhard) helps, they're a little more violent defensively, a little more athletic defensively. And then it's a top-flight offensive line, and then DJ Moore is going to make an impact."
What makes this exec think Buffalo, with Joe Brady replacing Sean McDermott as coach, can finally reach a Super Bowl with Josh Allen?
"Everybody is knocking him — 'He hasn't done it, hasn't done it,'" this exec said. "He did it in Kansas City in the championship game (in January 2022). It didn't end up the right way for him, but he did it."
Votes: 1-2-4-2-4-5 | Avg: 3.0 | Median: 3 | Vegas wins: 9.5 (T-5th-AFC)
Tier votes: SB contender: 5 | Division contender: 1
The top two teams in this AFC ranking appear strong on their offensive lines. That could help explain how Denver edged Houston for the second spot. Both are strong on defense.
"Sean Payton does a masterful job of making his teams feel they are better than where they are, and that exudes through their play," one exec said.
Support for Denver was not as strong as the Broncos' No. 2 ranking.
"As much as I don't buy Denver," one exec said, "they have the defense, they have the head coach, they have the quarterback (Bo Nix) healthy, they added Jaylen Waddle. I don't know about their run game or Houston's run game, but I trust the continuity of those defenses."
The one exec ranking Denver first in the AFC now thought that would likely change over the course of the season, but he wasn't willing to elevate teams with bigger question marks (Patrick Mahomes' health, for one, and the Bills' unproven head coach).
"I think when it's all said and done, Denver could be the third team in the AFC West," this exec said, "but going into the season, I give teams respect for what they have established."
Votes: 3-7-6-3-1-3 | Avg: 3.8 | Median: 3 | Vegas wins: 9.5 (T-5th-AFC)
Tier votes: SB contender: 4 | Division contender: 2
The Texans' roster is loved. Their quarterback is a question mark.
"I actually think the Texans might have the best roster (in the AFC)," one exec said. "I'd be tempted to put Houston above Buffalo because of that, but there is such a big difference in the quarterbacks."
The Texans have won a playoff game in each of the past three seasons, mostly on the strength of their defense. Their postseason defeats have shaken confidence around the league in C.J. Stroud.
"The last exposure to Houston was how badly they looked on offense," the exec slotting Houston sixth said. "I get it, Stroud is in Year 2 with the same coordinator (Nick Caley). But if he continues to look like he looked last year, they are going to have to win on defense, and I don't know how that is going to work. That is why I'm lower on them — nothing more, nothing less."
Stroud tossed four interceptions and took three sacks in Houston's 28-16 divisional playoff defeat to New England last season.
" I'm betting on the defense and just the maturation of where the team is at," the exec ranking Houston first in the conference said. "I think they are in that sweet spot where they take a step up. If you asked me to pick the AFC Championship Game, I would say Houston-Buffalo right now."
Votes: 4-3-9-4-3-6 | Avg: 4.8 | Median: 4 | Vegas wins: 10.5 (T-2nd-AFC)
Tier votes: SB contender: 4 | Division contender: 2
The Patriots reached the Super Bowl last season, but none of the execs has them among the top two in the conference now. None had New England in the top two last season.
"They faced a few quarterbacks last year that I did not even know who they were, and I work in the National Football League," one exec said.
Brady Cook, Dillon Gabriel, Quinn Ewers and Jarrett Stidham averaged 4.9 yards per pass attempt in four starts against New England last season (including playoffs). The Patriots also faced Justin Fields and Spencer Rattler, plus Geno Smith, Tua Tagovailoa, Jaxson Dart, Cam Ward and Joe Flacco.
"Cook? Who was that?" the exec added. "They play a tougher schedule this year, and frankly, their team is thin. The head coach said so himself."
Indeed, Mike Vrabel recently said he did not think New England had a very deep team.
"New England can take a drop because of the schedule, but they still have the Jets twice and Miami twice, and I like their coaching, so that's why I left them up there a little bit," one of the execs ranking New England third said.
The Patriots face the NFC North in the scheduling rotation this season.
"At some point, they are going to have to buck up and beat some good teams," another exec said. "I think they are the No. 1 regression team. Lastly, they haven't re-signed (Christian) Gonzalez yet. If that drags on into the season, it won't be good in the locker room."
Votes: 8-4-2-5-7-4 | Avg: 5.0 | Median: 4.5 | Vegas wins: 11.5 (1st-AFC)
Tier votes: SB contender: 4 | Division contender: 2
The Ravens were No. 1 in the AFC survey at this time last year. They finished ninth in the conference after quarterback Lamar Jackson and defensive tackle Nnamdi Madubuike suffered injuries early in the season. Jackson returned but wasn't a dynamic runner. Madubuike returned in time for training camp after rehabbing from what was initially considered a career-threatening neck injury, but it's not clear whether he will be ready to play in Week 1.
"I like that they are going to have a motivated Lamar Jackson," the exec slotting Baltimore second in the AFC said. "The offense and the offensive coordinator (Declan Doyle) will challenge him in a way he hasn't been challenged in quite some time."
The voter slotting Baltimore eighth did so because he has questions about Jackson after a disappointing 2025 season.
"So much depends on Lamar's health and explosion, which is such a question mark," the voter ranking Baltimore fifth said. "He did not play in preseason. It is all really projection. But how many two-time MVPs are out there? How do you not have them as a Super Bowl contender with him and Zay Flowers and Kyle Hamilton and Derrick Henry and Madubuike back?"
What about Doyle, the unproven offensive coordinator?
"You have to give Declan Doyle the benefit of the doubt with the Ben Johnson scheme, and Jesse Minter is obviously a really smart defensive coach," this exec added. "They are definitely in the mix, and they were a missed field goal away from making the playoffs last year, with everything that went wrong."
Votes: 5-5-3-9-5-7 | Avg: 5.7 | Median: 5 | Vegas wins: 10.5 (T-2nd-AFC)
Tier votes: SB contender: 1 | Division contender: 5
It's strange seeing the Chiefs all the way down here.
"Yeah, Andy Reid and a healthy Patrick Mahomes?" the exec slotting Kansas City third said. "I'll take my chances with them coming away with 11 wins."
That's barely higher than the Chiefs' Vegas win total, which ranks tied for second in the AFC.

full_text:
Last year, Tetairoa McMillan became the first Panthers player since Cam Newton in 2011 to be named Offensive Rookie of the Year. Jim Dedmon / Imagn Images
CHARLOTTE, N.C. — All of the attention on the Carolina Panthers’ wide receivers for the past week or so has focused on players at the bottom of the depth chart. That’s typical of the final week of training camp as teams prepared to make roster cuts.
Fans tend to enjoy reading roster projections and similar stories. But in the case of the Panthers’ receivers room, they ignored the guy at the top of the depth chart.
Now that it’s September, expect to start hearing a lot more about Tetairoa McMillan again.
McMillan put a bow on a fantastic first season Wednesday when he accepted his Rookie of the Year trophy from the Pro Football Writers of America. It will go on a mantle next to his AP Offensive Rookie of the Year award, though not on his mantle.
“My mom’s the one that likes to put the awards up in the house. I don’t really like having stuff of mine around the house, like pictures and stuff like that. I don’t know, just me I guess,” McMillan said. “No, all the awards is cool. I feel like I’ve been fortunate enough to win a lot of awards in my lifetime. So what’s another one, I guess.”
McMillan put together one of the most successful rookie seasons in franchise history after the Panthers drafted him eighth overall in 2025. He caught 70 passes for 1,014 yards to break Kelvin Benjamin’s team rookie receiving yardage record (1,008), and became the first Panthers player to win Offensive Rookie of the Year since Cam Newton in 2011.
AJ Dillon, the recently acquired running back, watched McMillan’s season from afar as a member of the Philadelphia Eagles. He arrived in Charlotte curious if he might find a receiver who was trending toward diva status, which is almost a rite of passage at the position.
“You would think a young guy, a lot of praise — the guy goes out there every day and goes all in, and looks amazing doing it,” Dillon said.
McMillan also looks bigger than he did a year ago, particularly in his lower body. He played every game as a rookie, but lost weight as the season wore on. McMillan added 17 pounds of muscle on his 6-foot-4 frame to get to 220, which Panthers coach Dave Canales believes will help him defeat press coverage and win battles downfield.
“He kinda was just a man on a mission to get stronger to be able to feel that power in his game. That really is a part of his game that needed to be addressed,” Canales said. “He really wanted to do that and he attacked it, put on some good, solid mass. He’s been great at the line of scrimmage, rugged to the ball. And he’s still got all the same (other) stuff, so I’m excited to see him this year.”
If McMillan finishes with at least the same number of catches, receiving yards and receiving touchdowns (7), he’ll become the fifth player in NFL history to reach those marks in each of his first two seasons. He’d join some impressive company: Marques Colston, Odell Beckham Jr., Justin Jefferson and Ja’Marr Chase are the others to do it.
“That’s a cool stat, by the way. But I feel like at the end of the day, you’re not able to achieve those stats if you’re not healthy,” McMillan said. “Everyone says they’ve got sophomore slumps and people get hurt and stuff like that. The main thing to be able to achieve those things is to be healthy. That’s all I can wish for.”
McMillan missed time during OTAs with a foot injury, but was on the field for every training camp practice. He and quarterback Bryce Young connected on a lot of scoring plays, at least until the offensive line was overmatched in a joint practice with the Houston Texans last week.
Dillon, who also spent time with the Green Bay Packers, said the 23-year-old McMillan’s physical gifts are just part of what makes him special.
“Wise beyond his years,” Dillon said. “He kind of has that poise where you would expect from a veteran guy. I know he’s going into Year 2 (after a) tremendous Year 1. Obviously, the football piece … he’s great. But my thing is his mindset. Nothing seems to rattle him. He goes out there and he just has fun.”
McMillan’s first NFL season was fun until it wasn’t. Twice this summer he’s mentioned the sting of a playoff loss to the Los Angeles Rams, who beat the Panthers 34-31 in the wild-card round behind a game-winning drive by Matthew Stafford.
Asked if he still thinks about the game, McMillan said: “I mean, I feel like it ain’t never left. I feel like it’s still here. … After that game, we all had that chip on our shoulder, ready to come into the 2026 season.”
McMillan has high hopes for the Panthers’ offense this year, calling it a “night and day” difference from last year’s.
“A lot more people are stepping up. We have a lot of dudes that can do a bunch of different things and are able to make plays wherever,” he explained. “We’ve got a deep tight end room, running back room, receiver room obviously.”
The Panthers are hoping to get contributions from Jalen Coker, Xavier Legette and others in Brad Idzik’s first season as the play caller. But the focal point of the offense will be McMillan, who will draw the most attention from defenses — and the media, now that those roster projection stories are done.
He wouldn’t want it any other way.
“Ain’t no pressure. That’s what they drafted me to be. That’s what they pay me all this money to do — just do my job and do it to the best of my ability,” he said. “Whether I’m the focal point one week or I’m the decoy the next week, as long as we do what we’re supposed to do, I’m not worried about it.”

A Lombardi Trophy — Super Bowl LIV — remains the centerpiece on the shelves behind Ryan Poles’ desk, a memento of the career achievement he experienced when, as assistant director of player personnel in Kansas City, he was part of the Chiefs’ climb to the NFL mountaintop in 2019.

full_text:
Quarterback Caleb Williams led the Bears to their first division title in seven years and followed it with a playoff win against the rival Packers. Todd Rosenberg / Getty Images
A Lombardi Trophy — Super Bowl LIV — remains the centerpiece on the shelves behind Ryan Poles’ desk, a memento of the career achievement he experienced when, as assistant director of player personnel in Kansas City, he was part of the Chiefs’ climb to the NFL mountaintop in 2019.
Still, the 3D-printed figurine to the right of that silver prize somehow feels more attention-grabbing inside the general manager’s office at Chicago Bears headquarters. Behind Poles, that is indeed plastic Ben Johnson, approximately 10 inches in height, shirtless and flexing with the city’s favorite new rallying cry — “Good, better, best” — in bold letters as the backdrop.
Who can forget that stirring moment from the locker room in Philadelphia last November when, after the Bears’ 24-15 beatdown of the Eagles, Johnson activated a free hot dog promotion at Chicago’s “The Wiener’s Circle” simply by baring his chest during the victory celebration?
Now Poles has a daily reminder behind him, even as he grins and swears he has no clue how the flexing Johnson action figure found its way to him. “It just showed up,” he says, amused by the serendipity.
That was not the case with the real Johnson, whose arrival in January 2025 came because Poles aggressively targeted him as the organization’s top choice to become the new coach. (And Johnson, with a strong desire for the Bears job, happily jumped into the boat.)
Now, the two men — coach and GM — are in the process of doing exactly as each promised when they were hired. Johnson, at his introductory news conference, promised to push and challenge players daily while significantly raising the standards and re-establishing a culture of accountability at Halas Hall.
Three years earlier, Poles announced his target with a bold vow that has echoed in these parts ever since.
We’re going to take the North and never give it back.
The taking of the NFC North finally happened last winter, at the end of Poles’ fourth season and with Johnson as a catalyst. Eleven regular-season wins — six in which the Bears trailed in the final two minutes — brought Chicago its first division title in seven years and just its sixth of the 21st century.
Johnson’s fingerprints were all over that emergence. Quarterback Caleb Williams made his impact felt, too. Now comes the oh-so-difficult task of “never giving it back,” the process of sustaining division success to keep the championships coming.
To that end, Poles is convinced Johnson’s presence will be the ultimate X-factor, giving the Bears a 750-horsepower engine for the NFL speedway.
In January, just days after the Bears’ magical 2025 dream run ended with a playoff loss, Poles was thrilled when Johnson slammed the back cover on that season and ordered everyone to start working for 2026.
“That desire to be great, to reinvent ourselves, to create our identity each and every year, that to me is the part where I really believe we’re in a good spot,” Poles told The Athletic last month. “I appreciate his leadership on that. It’s that mentality that allows you, I think, to keep stacking year after year after year. Because no one is satisfied.”
During his time in Kansas City’s front office, Poles was on the front end of a run in which the Chiefs won nine consecutive division titles. (They took the AFC West for the first time in 2016 — Poles was director of college scouting at that time — and didn’t give it back until last season.)
Coach Andy Reid had similar qualities to Johnson. Driven. Adaptable. Constantly looking to accentuate his team’s strengths while working to keep the group’s identity intact.
When the Chiefs’ first wave of success hit, Poles could feel the swell it put in the AFC West waters.
“There is a psychological advantage after you start stacking that success,” he said, “where teams are like, ‘Damn, we’ve got this team that won’t give it up.’ Psychologically, you kind of start defeating people before you even play.”
To that point, from 2016 to 2024, the Chiefs won 85 percent of their division games.
“Internally then,” Poles said, “there’s an expectation that we don’t lose divisional games.”
This Bears team, Poles acknowledges, is “not all the way there.”
As evidence, the Bears went 2-4 in NFC North games last season. “But,” Poles added, “the mentality we had then in Kansas City is what we’re trying to recreate here.”
Few organizations should understand the difficulty of sustaining high-level success quite like the Bears, who haven’t made the playoffs in three consecutive seasons since the 1980s.
Since the NFC North came into existence in 2002, the Bears have nearly twice as many last-place finishes (nine) as division titles. Still, at this spring’s league meetings in Phoenix, Bears chairman George McCaskey endorsed Johnson as exactly the kind of leader who can make the team’s “never give it back” dreams a reality, particularly after the coach so quickly archived the 2025 season by emphatically reminding everyone in the organization “there is no building off this.”
“We go back to square one,” Johnson stressed. “We’re back at the bottom again.”
Somehow, that sentiment fast became a supercharge of motivation rather than a buzzkill.
“I don’t think we have to worry about any complacency issues on coach Johnson’s watch,” McCaskey said.
Since 2002, when the NFL expanded to eight divisions, a dozen organizations have won at least three consecutive division crowns. It’s not a shocking list, headlined by the Patriots who won the AFC East 16 times across 17 seasons between 2003 and 2019. (The lone year they didn’t win the division in 2008, they went 11-5 and lost a conference-record decider — the fourth tiebreaker — with the Dolphins.)
The pairing of an elite quarterback in Tom Brady and a top-tier coach in Bill Belichick offered a fail-safe formula in New England. And that component of success should not be downplayed, particularly looking at a fraternity of quarterbacks to win at least three consecutive division titles since 2002, including MVP winners Brett Favre, Peyton Manning, Aaron Rodgers, Patrick Mahomes and Josh Allen, plus perennial Pro Bowlers like Drew Brees, Donovan McNabb and Philip Rivers.
The head coaches on the list include Sean Payton and Reid (in both Philadelphia and Kansas City).
To that end, the bond between Williams and Johnson feels like a significant tailwind for the Bears. The two have spent the last eight months publicly expressing their belief in one another and offering evidence that they are fully invested in their collective growth and single-minded in their pursuit of grand success.
“We have a real common goal,” Williams said. “And it’s to find a way to make the Chicago Bears champions.”
As gifted as Johnson is — as a communicator, as a leader, as a strategic visionary — the Bears’ ceiling for success may be defined most by Williams’ continued ascent. Yet through his own lens, Williams has been adamant that “coaching matters.” And the quarterback is in a wonderful headspace heading into this season with his trust in Johnson.
“Everything he says to me, I’ll do it at 200 percent and won’t look back,” Williams said.
Thus, even when the agitated version of Johnson surfaces and the coach becomes animated at miscues … “I know,” Williams said, “it’s for the greater good of the team.”
For Bears All-Pro guard Joe Thuney, the cultural currents that foster prolonged success should not be diminished. Thuney, entering his 11th season, has already won nine division championships while missing the playoffs just once.
He was with the Chiefs for four seasons (2021-24), adding two Super Bowl championships to the pair he won while with the Patriots (2016-20). Yes, Thuney had the luxury of blocking for Brady and Mahomes, two of the best quarterbacks of all time. But, Thuney said, another common denominator across both…

In the 2021 season, one year after drafting Joe Burrow, the Cincinnati Bengals found themselves in the franchise’s third Super Bowl. They followed that up with another AFC Championship Game appearance the next year. Since then, however, they’ve failed to make the playoffs.

full_text:
Cincinnati's passing game is in line for another productive season. Katie Stratman / Imagn Images via Reuters Connect
In the 2021 season, one year after drafting Joe Burrow, the Cincinnati Bengals found themselves in the franchise’s third Super Bowl. They followed that up with another AFC Championship Game appearance the next year. Since then, however, they’ve failed to make the playoffs.
In two of the last three years, Burrow’s season was shortened due to injury. He missed nine games in 2025 — Joe Flacco made more appearances for the Bengals — and to rub salt in the wound, the defensive unit finished 31st in the league in yards allowed and 32nd with 60 touchdowns surrendered.
Cincinnati ventures into this season having made multiple improvements. Burrow is healthy. Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins are still young and playing at elite levels. Veteran tackles Dexter Lawrence and Jonathan Allen beef up a defense that ranked last in rushing yards allowed, while Super Bowl winner Boye Mafe brings explosiveness off the edge.
But as Bengals fans know all too well, this season rests on whether Burrow can stay healthy.
To keep up with Joe Cool and company, we’ve compiled a guide for the Bengals’ upcoming campaign. Whether you are Ohio through and through or a fan on the move, we’ve got you and the Bengals covered on The Athletic . Just make sure to follow beat reporter Paul Dehner Jr ., who’s covered the team and the NFL since 2009.
All times listed below are ET.
The most expansive option for live game coverage is a multichannel plan. That includes streamers like Fubo, Sling TV and YouTube TV, or more traditional providers like DirecTV, Dish and Xfinity. We lay out cord-cutting alternatives for each NFL media partner down below, but there’s a certain peace of mind to the consolidation of pay television.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, AFC Championship Game
Each week, CBS carries games across two Sunday kickoff slots: one at 1 p.m., and another at 4:05 p.m. or the national window at 4:25 p.m. There will be 10 nationwide Sunday doubleheaders this year on CBS. Broadcasts are set by region when there are multiple offerings in a spot.
It’s not a clean split, but CBS is known as the primary home of the AFC. The network’s theme music is a certified slapper.
Its main pregame show, “The NFL Today,” adds recent retirees Russell Wilson and Kyle Long to its studio crew. CBS announcers include Jim Nantz and Ian Eagle, while the color commentary rotation stars JJ Watt.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an indoor TV antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local CBS games also stream on Paramount+.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, NFC Championship Game
Like CBS, Fox splits Sunday afternoons between early 1 p.m. action and later 4:05/4:25 p.m. matchups. Its centerpiece is branded as “America’s Game of the Week.” Unlike CBS, Fox has a dancing robot named Cleatus . It’s the nominal network for the NFC as well.
Kevin Burkhardt, Joe Davis and Adam Amin are the lead play-by-play voices. Burkhardt pairs with Tom Brady, while Davis calls games alongside Greg Olsen. Amin is partnered with newcomer Drew Brees, who is fresh off his Pro Football Hall of Fame induction. Some Spanish-language broadcasts are available on Fox Deportes.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local Fox games also stream on Fox One.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (out-of-market fans)
These two are the access points for all non-national matchups that aren’t on regional CBS or Fox.
NFL Sunday Ticket has full games. It’s exclusive to YouTube and YouTube TV. Those without a YouTube TV plan can still get NFL Sunday Ticket as a primetime channel through the standard YouTube app.
RedZone is the whip-around program that jumps around the slate to cover scoring drives. This is the place for Scott Hanson , “the witching hour” and chaotic octobox split screens. It can be added to NFL Sunday Ticket, and it’s included on some high-end pay TV sports plans.
RedZone also lives on NFL+ Premium, which can be bundled with the ESPN Unlimited plan.
What you’ll need to watch: An NFL Sunday Ticket subscription through YouTube TV or the YouTube app; NFL RedZone access through select pay TV packages, ESPN Unlimited or NFL+ Premium.
Playoffs: 2 wild-card games, 1 divisional game
This is the faithful home of “Sunday Night Football” each weekend. And because everything has to be confusing, the NBC lineup opens with a Wednesday night season premiere. At least SNF has a consistent 8:20 p.m. start time.
Mike Tirico and Cris Collinsworth are in the booth, with Melissa Stark reporting from the sidelines. Carrie Underwood sings about waiting all day for Sunday night . NBC’s “Football Night in America” pregame show brings on longtime head coach (and Bengals final boss) Mike Tomlin. Telemundo has the telecasts in Spanish.
The network has two extra Saturday offerings for Week 17. One is exclusive to Peacock, and both matchups will be announced later in the season. The same goes for NBC’s Week 18 regular-season finale.
“Sunday Night Football” is subject to flex scheduling — games can be swapped in and out of the window twice between Weeks 5-10 and any time from Weeks 11-17. This allows executives to pick games with greater playoff implications, though it leaves the actual ticket holders in a bind.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing, or a Peacock account with the live sports plan.
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, Super Bowl LXI
The Disney networks combine to cover 17 “Monday Night Football” games. Ten of those are on both ABC and ESPN, with another seven exclusive to the latter. The oft-maligned “Monday Night Football” doubleheader is now a thing of the past.
MNF kickoffs have 8:15 p.m. starts, and their schedule flexes can happen any time in Weeks 12-17. The two Saturday ABC/ESPN matchups in Week 18 will be set as the postseason picture sharpens.
ESPN is preparing for its first Super Bowl broadcast ever on Feb. 14, 2027. It will be simulcast on ABC.
Joe Buck handles play-by-play for MNF. He’s joined by analyst Troy Aikman, plus the sideline duo of Lisa Salters and Laura Rutledge. Spanish-language airings can be found on ESPN Deportes. For 12 regular-season games and the Super Bowl, ESPN2 offers an alternate “ManningCast,” in which Eli and Peyton Manning watch the games with famous fans. Guests have ranged from Bill Belichick to Lil Wayne .
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for ABC, or an ESPN Unlimited account.
Main window: Thursday night
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game
Most weeks begin with “Thursday Night Football,” which kicks off at 8:15 p.m. Those games are behind the Prime paywall, but they’re free over the air in the participants’ home markets. Flex rules around TNF are a bit less hectic, with two allotments between Weeks 13-17.
The Bengals are currently set to host the final TNF game of the regular season, which pits them against the hated Baltimore Ravens on New Year’s Eve.
Thursdays are called by Al Michaels and Kirk Herbstreit, with Kaylee Hartung on sideline duty. Herbstreit loves dogs ; Michaels hates vegetables . Prime has Spanish-language coverage and advanced stat broadcast options within its app. One-time Bengals quarterback Ryan Fitzpatrick and “ Ruler of the Jungle ” and former captain Andrew Whitworth are among the pregame and postgame personalities.
What you’ll need to watch: Amazon Prime. TNF is also free on Twitch with a registered account.
The league-owned media outlet is now under ESPN’s purview, thanks to a blockbuster deal that gave the NFL a 10 percent ownership stake in “The Worldwide Leader in Sports.” As of July 30, NFL Network is integrated into the ESPN Unlimited plan. It can also be accessed through NFL+ or NFL+ Premium.

full_text:
Erick All Jr.'s truly dangerous skill set allows Cincinnati to shift in ways it can’t with any other player on the roster. Sam Greene / The Enquirer via USA Network
CINCINNATI — Erick All Jr. was worried. He started to see signs of caution from the Cincinnati Bengals coaching staff this month.
Caution and concern had hovered over him for years as he battled injuries throughout every step of his career. They’ve defined him since November 2024, when he tore his ACL, a career-threatening knee injury that cost him a season-and-a-half.
Everyone always wants to know how he’s feeling. All just wants to play football.
Finally cleared this offseason to fully do so and strapping on the pads again, the last thing the Bengals tight end wanted to hear was that he was being held out of any games, practices or even drills.
Imposed limitations along the way have all been part of the plan to gradually return All to full force without going too fast.
“I definitely sense it,” tight ends coach James Casey said. “He tells me all the time.”
Head coach Zac Taylor once said if you looked up the word “physical” in the dictionary, it would just be a picture of All.
“He’s trying to put his face through somebody’s soul,” Taylor said.
These days, with the opener and a long-desired return to football 10 days away, All seems less demonic and more like a pit bull on a leash. He’s been pulled back by trainers with two hands, with wide eyes fixed on the pigskin in front of him.
Enough limitations. Enough caution.
“Just throw me in the yard and let me run,” All said. “I’m tired of this injury s—.”
There are two schools of thought for All’s return through the early portions of this season.
1. Throw him in yard, full go, no more limiting, no snap counts, no concern for opponent’s souls and fully unleash the 25-year-old coming off two ACL surgeries while everyone crosses fingers that his ligaments hold up.
2. Use a touch-and-go approach of giving him a role and expanding it as he handles his assignments each game.
I posed both of those options to Taylor. He did not hesitate to share his choice.
“The first one,” he said. “The first one.”
Taylor left no doubt. Coaches have used caution. They’ve been focused on gradually working him up to the games. All will now get his wish. No more holding back, which was breaking news for the 2024 fourth-round pick on Tuesday.
“Honestly, I had no idea,” he said. “I kind of got worried they were going to (limit me). I’m glad they are not doing that. Because I was getting some work during camp, but I kind of felt like I needed more, so it feels good to hear that.”
That’s a much sweeter sound to All than the clatter of a vehicle knocking him to the ground on the streets of Greece this summer.
All reiterated this week that he feels “100 percent, for sure.” But that doesn’t mean his path over the last month was perfect.
“There are some days where my knee feels a little weird or a little different,” he said, “but it is still healing and everything is good.”
That’s part of what made the limitations during a few days or drills and only playing six preseason snaps extra concerning and frustrating for the 25-year-old. He’s dying to work through those.
“It was a point to where they sat me down, I sat down for a little week or so,” All said. “I missed a couple practices where I felt like I could do something, where I wanted to play through that kind of soreness in my knee.”
That’s what All does. You can’t coach that out of him. That’s how he views football and plays the game. That’s why Taylor knows there really can’t be restrictions on a player that could easily be viewed as the breakout X-factor of the 2026 Bengals offense.
“You tell a guy to run full speed and run into a wall, it’s like most guys are not gonna really do that,” Casey said. “He’s the guy; he will run right through the wall.”
The second coming of the under-center-All offense awaits his return. The Bengals made no secret of its installation and their re-dedication to using the under-center and play-action chapter of the playbook this offseason and in training camp. The last time they truly used it in the regular season was when All emerged as a rookie.
“It was fun to see in ‘24,” Casey said. “I thought it was justified because of how well he was doing out there when he was playing.”
He was the key to unlocking their ability to play that way. Without him after the injury, they returned to their spread, 11-personnel past.
The concern of the coaching staff — and everyone invested in his future — was that he wouldn’t look the same this camp. Would he be a step slower or unable to cut in the same fashion? Sure, he would still have his patented appetite for physicality, but would the explosion be the same?
Casey suppressed concern and replaced it with excitement, as a former player himself who sees the same intensity and recklessness he prided himself on playing with in his star pupil.
“Running his routes is probably the most impressive thing for me,” Casey said. “He can run, he’s back to Erick.”
The other tight ends for the Bengals aren’t as well-rounded as All. His truly dangerous skill set allows Cincinnati to shift in ways it can’t with any other player on the roster. They would love to have that option.
Considering All’s mentality, there can only be one way to find out, and only one way he wants to find out: Take off the leash and throw him in the yard. He’s tired of this injury s—.

full_text:
From left, Cowboys receivers KaVontae Turpin, George Pickens and CeeDee Lamb are three reasons there's optimism as the season opener nears. Kirby Lee / Imagn Images
There’s a misconception out there that every year the Dallas Cowboys are overhyped and that every year is “their year.”
So when there are times like the last seven months and positive vibes surround the team, many suggest they hear these things every year.
That’s simply not true. No realistic observer was saying that about the Cowboys two years ago, fresh off that disastrous playoff loss to the Green Bay Packers. And it certainly wasn’t being said during all of the Micah Parsons contract drama heading into last season.
But the hype is there with this current team, and deservedly so. Now, that’s not to say they are Super Bowl favorites. Recent oddsmakers have them just outside the top 10. They are, however, a team that has everything needed to make the playoffs and potentially get hot at the most important time. That hasn’t happened in the last 30 years, so many won’t believe it until they see it. Completely understandable. Most likely felt the same way about the New York Knicks entering last season.
This story is not designed to explain why this is finally the Cowboys’ year. This is just to break down why things have felt different coming out of training camp.
Jerry Jones is very open about saying when things get slow, he’ll stir it up. The Cowboys owner and general manager talked with reporters several times while the team held its annual training camp in Oxnard, Calif. Jones did not stir anything up.
George Pickens’ contract situation had the potential to be something that turned into a distraction. But not only did Pickens sign the franchise tag and show up to camp , he participated in every practice and was the team’s top performer. It was a much different situation than with Parsons a year ago, when it was unclear when Parsons would practice and play Week 1. He was eventually traded a week before the start of the season, which unquestionably put Dallas’ defense in a position to struggle.
With Jones, there’s always the chance he could say or do something to make headlines and possibly cause a distraction. But lately, he seems on board with riding some calmer waves.
Superstition and sports go hand in hand. Cowboys coach Brian Schottenheimer wanted to change the subject when this topic was brought up late in camp. The Cowboys have been fortunate in the health department. They are entering the regular season about as healthy as can be. Backup defensive tackle Jonathan Bullard has been working off to the side on resistance cords, but he’s expected to be ready for the start of the season. Reserve outside linebacker Marist Liufau fractured his left forearm in Dallas’ final preseason game, but he is expected to return at some point this season. Other than that, it’s a healthy roster.
There are many reasons for that, ranging from their work on two very well-maintained grass practice fields in Oxnard to an emphasis on not tackling to the ground in any part of camp practices. It was rare to see a bunch of bodies on the ground near the line of scrimmage during the 15 camp practices. Since returning to The Star, they’ve practiced earlier in the morning to avoid the Texas heat and work on their outdoor grass practice field.
There’s only so much that can be done to prevent injuries in such a violent sport, but the Cowboys have done as good a job as possible to make it to Week 1 in outstanding health.
This isn’t to say players were visibly out on the coaching staffs in previous training camps, but this year’s group seems even more locked in on what the coaches are preaching. The offense is entering Year 2 with Schottenheimer calling plays and Klayton Adams as coordinator. They appear to be building on what was already one of the NFL’s best offenses. Defensively is where the bigger jump is expected. Christian Parker appears to have that side of the ball bought in on his new scheme and approach. It also helps that there is quality leadership from veterans like Quinnen Williams and Kenny Clark down to rookies like Caleb Downs. This isn’t to say the expectations should be a top-10 defense, but this does look like a group that will be significantly improved from last season.
Entering camp, there were concerns about starting left tackle, inside linebacker, outside linebacker and cornerback. Entering Week 1, the two biggest questions are starting right tackle and the depth on the offensive line. Terence Steele is expected to remain the starter, but competition was added with the trade for Broderick Jones. Defensively, the play of Shavon Revel, DeMarvion Overshown, Jaishawn Barham and Rashan Gary, coupled with the signing of Von Miller, has helped alleviate some of those other concerns. Cornerback and inside linebacker depth could be better, but the overall defensive roster looks like it could be pretty good.
For too long, defensive tackle and safety were two of their biggest weaknesses. Over the last year, both have become strengths.
Offensively, as long as the line gives Dak Prescott a little time, he should be able to put up a lot of points with CeeDee Lamb, George Pickens, Ryan Flournoy, Javonte Williams, Jake Ferguson, KaVontae Turpin and Brevyn Spann-Ford.
It genuinely feels like if the right move is there, they would part with early picks in next year’s draft to try to win now. Maybe that’s another edge rusher. Maybe it’s another cornerback. Maybe nothing happens at all. But this year, it seems more possible than in most previous seasons that they are open to taking a little bit of a future gamble to win now.

"Duuuuuval!" — Trevor Lawrence, probably. Courtney Culbreath / Getty Images
They’re on the prowl and they’re hungry, too!
The Jacksonville Jaguars assume their posts as reigning AFC South champions, with a fair shot at repeating . Liam Coen’s team finished 2025 with top-10 rankings in both scoring offense and defense. Almost all of the main contributors are back for 2026 as well.
Trevor Lawrence is coming off the most assured season of his pro career. He’s surrounded by talented, diverse receivers, including Jakobi Meyers, Brian Thomas Jr. and Parker Washington. The pass rush is fronted by Josh Hines-Allen and Travon Walker. If running back Bhayshul Tuten can build on his strong playoff showing alongside free-agent addition Chris Rodriguez Jr., and if mystery box Travis Hunter can put it all together, then the Jags are going to be a problem.
Once again , Jacksonville’s schedule includes a London stretch, with a Week 5 game versus the Philadelphia Eagles and a Week 6 follow-up with the rival Houston Texans. The Jaguars are also slated for three primetime matchups against the Baltimore Ravens (Week 9), Pittsburgh Steelers (Week 14) and Dallas Cowboys (Week 16). Fans can refresh on the local and national broadcast situations below. Be sure to follow JAX on The Athletic , too.
All times listed below are ET.
The most expansive option for live game coverage is a multichannel plan. That includes streamers like Fubo, Sling TV and YouTube TV, or more traditional providers like DirecTV, Dish and Xfinity. We lay out cord-cutting alternatives for each NFL media partner down below, but there’s a certain peace of mind to the consolidation of pay television.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, AFC Championship Game

It’s not a clean split, but CBS is known as the primary home of the AFC and is currently scheduled to carry eight Jags games. The network’s theme music is also a certified slapper.
Its main pregame show, “The NFL Today,” adds recent retirees Russell Wilson and Kyle Long to its studio crew. CBS announcers include Jim Nantz and Ian Eagle, while the color commentary rotation stars JJ Watt.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an indoor TV antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local CBS games also stream on Paramount+.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, NFC Championship Game
Like CBS, Fox splits Sunday afternoons between early 1 p.m. action and later 4:05/4:25 p.m. matchups. Its centerpiece is branded as “America’s Game of the Week.” Unlike CBS, Fox has a dancing robot named Cleatus . It’s the nominal network for the NFC as well.
Kevin Burkhardt, Joe Davis and Adam Amin are the lead play-by-play voices. Burkhardt pairs with Tom Brady, while Davis calls games alongside Greg Olsen. summary:

full_text:
Josh Allen enters his first NFL season without Sean McDermott as his head coach, as Joe Brady takes over. Jason Miller / Getty Images
After ranking NFC teams 1-16 on Wednesday , six NFL team executives are back to stack the AFC as the 2026 regular season approaches.
Is this finally the Buffalo Bills’ year? Four of the six execs have Buffalo at the top. In a change, the Chiefs failed to crack the top five. Are they too low?
We answer those questions and more in a run-through of all 16 teams, from Buffalo to Miami, ranked below in median order, with average as a tiebreaker.
Votes: 2-1-1-1-2-1 | Avg: 1.3 | Median: 1 | Vegas wins: 10.5 (T-2nd-AFC)
Tier votes: SB contender: 6
The Bills top the AFC this year almost by default amid perceptions that Kansas City and Baltimore have regressed, while Denver and New England remain a tick behind.
"Josh Allen is the best player in the league," one exec said.
While some criticized the price Buffalo paid in the offseason when acquiring DJ Moore from Chicago, one of the execs in this survey said he expected big things from the receiver in Buffalo.
"My hardest choice was Houston-Buffalo (for the top spot)," another exec said. "The defensive change (under new coordinator Jim Leonhard) helps, they're a little more violent defensively, a little more athletic defensively. And then it's a top-flight offensive line, and then DJ Moore is going to make an impact."
What makes this exec think Buffalo, with Joe Brady replacing Sean McDermott as coach, can finally reach a Super Bowl with Josh Allen?
"Everybody is knocking him — 'He hasn't done it, hasn't done it,'" this exec said. "He did it in Kansas City in the championship game (in January 2022). It didn't end up the right way for him, but he did it."
Votes: 1-2-4-2-4-5 | Avg: 3.0 | Median: 3 | Vegas wins: 9.5 (T-5th-AFC)
Tier votes: SB contender: 5 | Division contender: 1
The top two teams in this AFC ranking appear strong on their offensive lines. That could help explain how Denver edged Houston for the second spot. Both are strong on defense.
"Sean Payton does a masterful job of making his teams feel they are better than where they are, and that exudes through their play," one exec said.
Support for Denver was not as strong as the Broncos' No. 2 ranking.
"As much as I don't buy Denver," one exec said, "they have the defense, they have the head coach, they have the quarterback (Bo Nix) healthy, they added Jaylen Waddle. I don't know about their run game or Houston's run game, but I trust the continuity of those defenses."
The one exec ranking Denver first in the AFC now thought that would likely change over the course of the season, but he wasn't willing to elevate teams with bigger question marks (Patrick Mahomes' health, for one, and the Bills' unproven head coach).
"I think when it's all said and done, Denver could be the third team in the AFC West," this exec said, "but going into the season, I give teams respect for what they have established."
Votes: 3-7-6-3-1-3 | Avg: 3.8 | Median: 3 | Vegas wins: 9.5 (T-5th-AFC)
Tier votes: SB contender: 4 | Division contender: 2
The Texans' roster is loved. Their quarterback is a question mark.
"I actually think the Texans might have the best roster (in the AFC)," one exec said. "I'd be tempted to put Houston above Buffalo because of that, but there is such a big difference in the quarterbacks."
The Texans have won a playoff game in each of the past three seasons, mostly on the strength of their defense. Their postseason defeats have shaken confidence around the league in C.J. Stroud.
"The last exposure to Houston was how badly they looked on offense," the exec slotting Houston sixth said. "I get it, Stroud is in Year 2 with the same coordinator (Nick Caley). But if he continues to look like he looked last year, they are going to have to win on defense, and I don't know how that is going to work. That is why I'm lower on them — nothing more, nothing less."
Stroud tossed four interceptions and took three sacks in Houston's 28-16 divisional playoff defeat to New England last season.
" I'm betting on the defense and just the maturation of where the team is at," the exec ranking Houston first in the conference said. "I think they are in that sweet spot where they take a step up. If you asked me to pick the AFC Championship Game, I would say Houston-Buffalo right now."
Votes: 4-3-9-4-3-6 | Avg: 4.8 | Median: 4 | Vegas wins: 10.5 (T-2nd-AFC)
Tier votes: SB contender: 4 | Division contender: 2
The Patriots reached the Super Bowl last season, but none of the execs has them among the top two in the conference now. None had New England in the top two last season.
"They faced a few quarterbacks last year that I did not even know who they were, and I work in the National Football League," one exec said.
Brady Cook, Dillon Gabriel, Quinn Ewers and Jarrett Stidham averaged 4.9 yards per pass attempt in four starts against New England last season (including playoffs). The Patriots also faced Justin Fields and Spencer Rattler, plus Geno Smith, Tua Tagovailoa, Jaxson Dart, Cam Ward and Joe Flacco.
"Cook? Who was that?" the exec added. "They play a tougher schedule this year, and frankly, their team is thin. The head coach said so himself."
Indeed, Mike Vrabel recently said he did not think New England had a very deep team.
"New England can take a drop because of the schedule, but they still have the Jets twice and Miami twice, and I like their coaching, so that's why I left them up there a little bit," one of the execs ranking New England third said.
The Patriots face the NFC North in the scheduling rotation this season.
"At some point, they are going to have to buck up and beat some good teams," another exec said. "I think they are the No. 1 regression team. Lastly, they haven't re-signed (Christian) Gonzalez yet. If that drags on into the season, it won't be good in the locker room."
Votes: 8-4-2-5-7-4 | Avg: 5.0 | Median: 4.5 | Vegas wins: 11.5 (1st-AFC)
Tier votes: SB contender: 4 | Division contender: 2
The Ravens were No. 1 in the AFC survey at this time last year. They finished ninth in the conference after quarterback Lamar Jackson and defensive tackle Nnamdi Madubuike suffered injuries early in the season. Jackson returned but wasn't a dynamic runner. Madubuike returned in time for training camp after rehabbing from what was initially considered a career-threatening neck injury, but it's not clear whether he will be ready to play in Week 1.
"I like that they are going to have a motivated Lamar Jackson," the exec slotting Baltimore second in the AFC said. "The offense and the offensive coordinator (Declan Doyle) will challenge him in a way he hasn't been challenged in quite some time."
The voter slotting Baltimore eighth did so because he has questions about Jackson after a disappointing 2025 season.
"So much depends on Lamar's health and explosion, which is such a question mark," the voter ranking Baltimore fifth said. "He did not play in preseason. It is all really projection. But how many two-time MVPs are out there? How do you not have them as a Super Bowl contender with him and Zay Flowers and Kyle Hamilton and Derrick Henry and Madubuike back?"
What about Doyle, the unproven offensive coordinator?
"You have to give Declan Doyle the benefit of the doubt with the Ben Johnson scheme, and Jesse Minter is obviously a really smart defensive coach," this exec added. "They are definitely in the mix, and they were a missed field goal away from making the playoffs last year, with everything that went wrong."
Votes: 5-5-3-9-5-7 | Avg: 5.7 | Median: 5 | Vegas wins: 10.5 (T-2nd-AFC)
Tier votes: SB contender: 1 | Division contender: 5
It's strange seeing the Chiefs all the way down here.
"Yeah, Andy Reid and a healthy Patrick Mahomes?" the exec slotting Kansas City third said. "I'll take my chances with them coming away with 11 wins."
That's barely higher than the Chiefs' Vegas win total, which ranks tied for second in the AFC.

title: How the Patriots are looking to bounce back from last season's Super Bowl loss Vrabel and the team will try to put together another successful season while picking up the pieces from a Super Bowl loss. It won't be easy. Chad Graff 5
summary:
Mike Vrabel and the Patriots went 14-3 last year and won three playoff games before losing in the Super Bowl. Getting back to the big game will be even tougher this fall. Nick Cammett / Getty Images
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — A Super Bowl rematch looms in Week 1 for the New England Patriots, an odd Wednesday kickoff against the Seattle Seahawks that presents a truncated schedule and dictates additional reps in preparation.
At one point, the Patriots moved the offense to an indoor bubble where music bla
full_text:
Mike Vrabel and the Patriots went 14-3 last year and won three playoff games before losing in the Super Bowl. Getting back to the big game will be even tougher this fall. Nick Cammett / Getty Images
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — A Super Bowl rematch looms in Week 1 for the New England Patriots, an odd Wednesday kickoff against the Seattle Seahawks that presents a truncated schedule and dictates additional reps in preparation.
At one point, the Patriots moved the offense to an indoor bubble where music blared, an attempt to get used to calling plays in the loud environment that’s expected on Sept. 9 when the Seahawks unveil their championship banner. At another, New England installed plays specifically for Seattle’s complex defense, the one that gave the Pats fits in February.
But for the most part, the Patriots were focused on themselves. Camp is for determining the best players on the roster and ensuring everyone is on the same page. So it wasn’t the time for early game-planning for the Seahawks or taking a trip down memory lane.
“I think you just have to be careful,” coach Mike Vrabel said, explaining why he hasn’t been all in on Seahawks prep in recent weeks. “It’s the first game. They’ve got a new coordinator, and some things will be different. I’m sure they’ll have some plays that are similar (to last year) that they like, and I think their defensive structure may be the same, (but) it may not. … You just have to be careful how much you show them and try to focus on what it is that we’re trying to accomplish.”
If you zoom out, though, what’s more interesting is how the Patriots are navigating the challenge of putting together another successful season while picking up the pieces from a Super Bowl loss. History shows it could be rocky.
Four of the last seven Super Bowl losers missed the playoffs the next season, including the last two (the Kansas City Chiefs and the San Francisco 49ers). The 2018 Patriots are the only team this century to win the Super Bowl following a loss in the title game the season before. This century, 15 of the 25 Super Bowl losers failed to make the playoffs the following season.
So how are the Patriots addressing that? Mostly by operating with a business-as-usual approach. They haven’t had extensive conversations about the loss to the Seahawks. Vrabel said he didn’t seek out advice this offseason from others who have lost in the Super Bowl.
“We have a lot of new guys on the roster,” he said. “We have guys that are returning, our core guys, and understand that the journey’s going to be a lot more difficult just based on how we finished. … I think just staying consistent is probably the thing that we have to continue to do and not ride the waves of up here and then down low. We just have to try to stay consistent and continue to improve. The teams that do that are usually the ones that play in January.”
New players haven’t sensed any wariness from the loss or felt a Super Bowl hangover. And New England has plenty of new players to help improve on last season; the team will take six new starters to Seattle for the opener. The Patriots also have 11 rookies on the roster, which suggests that this is a different group.
“We’re not trying to recreate that magic,” new safety and co-captain Kevin Byard said. “This is a whole new situation with new guys that are going to have to win a different way than they won last year.”
Of course, it’s easy to say the Patriots have moved on from the Super Bowl. It’s another thing to have the tough task of heading to Seattle for the opener — and watching the Seahawks unfurl a banner commemorating their championship.
This marks only the second time since 1970 that the NFL season is beginning with a Super Bowl rematch. In 2016, the Denver Broncos beat the Carolina Panthers in Week 1, celebrating a second straight win over Carolina, this time on banner night.
“There’ll be a lot of energy there,” Vrabel said in preparation for next week. “We’ll have to be ready for the environment, and we’ll have to be really sound in our operation and everything that we do. The magnitude of it is always important. … It’ll be a great test and a great challenge for us to go on the road and do that early in the season.”
It will also be a great test to see how much has actually changed for the Patriots. The assumption is that the O-line will be better, that A.J. Brown will add a new dimension to the passing game and that the defensive secondary will make up for questions about the pass rush. Who better to test those assumptions against than the team that dominated them in the Super Bowl? And what better way to find out if this group can make a return trip to the big game?
“We’re focused on just competing against Seattle,” Vrabel said, “not competing for something that’s going to happen in February.”

full_text:
Baker Mayfield and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers are favored to beat out reigning NFC South champions Bryce Young and the Carolina Panthers for the division crown in 2026. Julio Aguilar / Getty Images
Single-digit wins have been enough to claim the NFC South crown in three of the past four seasons — and it’ll likely be enough to do it again in 2026.
The Athletic ‘s predictive analyst Austin Mock forecasts all four teams to finish with between six and eight wins while sportsbooks like DraftKings list odds that give each between an 18 and 35 percent implied probability to come out on top. Let’s take a look at the board, then dive into Mock’s projections and his take on what will be the tightest (if weakest) division race of the NFL season.
The NFC South is such a toss up — no team stands head and shoulders above the rest, which means all four are capable of winning the division.
I mostly agree that the Bucs should be considered the favorites going into the season. They have arguably the best quarterback in the division, maybe even the best overall roster. But at this point, am I trusting them without longtime stars Mike Evans and Lavonte David? How do they replace those guys? There is some serious uncertainty there.
I’m not sure I’m a believer in the Panthers just yet given their uncertainty at offensive tackle, but they are still capable of winning this division about one-fifth of the time.
I was quite excited about the Saints and their offense under head coach Kellen Moore this time last month, but it doesn’t look like first-round rookie wide receiver Jordyn Tyson will be ready anytime soon.
Meanwhile, the Falcons have yet to pick a Week 1 starter from their crowded quarterback room .
I’m not very confident in any of these teams, so calling this the tightest division in the NFL is pretty spot on — even if it’s because it’s the worst in football.
Last season, the Panthers claimed the crown after winning only eight games by emerging from a three-way tiebreaker. This season, I firmly believe eight wins could once again be enough for any of these teams to take the title. My model believes every NFC South team is a below-average NFL team, all sitting within two points of each other from a power rating perspective.

full_text:
Last year, Breece Hall topped 1,000 rushing yards for the first time in his NFL career. Evan Bernstein / Getty Images
The New York Jets went 3-14 in their first season under Aaron Glenn, extending the NFL’s longest active playoff drought to 15 seasons. Will the Jets make it any easier to be a fan this year?
The reset started before last season even ended. At the trade deadline, the Jets dealt cornerback Sauce Gardner and defensive tackle Quinnen Williams. Turnover continued in the offseason, including a March trade that sent edge rusher Jermaine Johnson to the Tennessee Titans for 366-pound nose tackle T’Vondre Sweat.
Glenn and general manager Darren Mougey return for their second season together, but the coaching staff has changed around them. Frank Reich is the new offensive coordinator, while Brian Duker takes over as defensive coordinator. Glenn will call the defensive plays himself this season after saying he missed doing so in 2025.
Geno Smith is back at quarterback a decade after leaving the Jets. He’ll have something to work with: Breece Hall is coming off his first 1,000-yard rushing season, and the sure-handed Garrett Wilson remains the top receiving threat. The offensive line is still young, but continuity gives the group a stronger foundation than it had a year ago.
On defense, New York added veteran safety Minkah Fitzpatrick and brought linebacker Demario Davis back for a third stint with the franchise, while edge rusher David Bailey arrives as the No. 2 overall pick.
The Jets’ television schedule is weirdly simple, at least before any possible flexes. New York does not have a primetime game scheduled; all eight home kickoffs are at 1 p.m. local time, and its first 16 games are split between CBS and Fox. Only the Week 18 trip to the Buffalo Bills remains TBD. The season also opens in Tennessee against former Jets head coach Robert Saleh.
Make sure you’re following the Jets and senior writer Zack Rosenblatt on The Athletic for year-round coverage.
All times listed below are ET.
The most expansive option for live game coverage is a multichannel plan. That includes streamers like Fubo, Sling TV and YouTube TV, or more traditional providers like DirecTV, Dish and Xfinity. We lay out cord-cutting alternatives for each NFL media partner down below, but there’s a certain peace of mind to the consolidation of pay television.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, AFC Championship Game
Each week, CBS carries games across two Sunday kickoff slots: one at 1 p.m., and another at 4:05 p.m. or the national window at 4:25 p.m. There will be 10 nationwide Sunday doubleheaders this year on CBS. Broadcasts are set by region when there are multiple offerings in a spot.
It’s not a clean split, but CBS is known as the primary home of the AFC. The network’s theme music is a certified slapper.
Its main pregame show, “The NFL Today,” adds recent retirees Russell Wilson and Kyle Long to its studio crew. CBS announcers include Jim Nantz and Ian Eagle, while the color commentary rotation stars JJ Watt.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an indoor TV antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local CBS games also stream on Paramount+.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, NFC Championship Game
Like CBS, Fox splits Sunday afternoons between early 1 p.m. action and later 4:05/4:25 p.m. matchups. Its centerpiece is branded as “America’s Game of the Week.” Unlike CBS, Fox has a dancing robot named Cleatus . It’s the nominal network for the NFC as well.
Kevin Burkhardt, Joe Davis and Adam Amin are the lead play-by-play voices. Burkhardt pairs with Jets heel Tom Brady, while Davis calls games alongside Greg Olsen. Amin is partnered with newcomer Drew Brees, who is fresh off his Pro Football Hall of Fame induction. Some Spanish-language broadcasts are available on Fox Deportes.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local Fox games also stream on Fox One.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (out-of-market fans)
These two are the access points for all non-national matchups that aren’t on regional CBS or Fox.
NFL Sunday Ticket has full games. It’s exclusive to YouTube and YouTube TV. Those without a YouTube TV plan can still get NFL Sunday Ticket as a primetime channel through the standard YouTube app.
RedZone is the whip-around program that jumps around the slate to cover scoring drives. This is the place for Scott Hanson , “the witching hour” and chaotic octobox split screens. It can be added to NFL Sunday Ticket, and it’s included on some high-end pay TV sports plans.
RedZone also lives on NFL+ Premium, which can be bundled with the ESPN Unlimited plan.
What you’ll need to watch: An NFL Sunday Ticket subscription through YouTube TV or the YouTube app; NFL RedZone access through select pay TV packages, ESPN Unlimited or NFL+ Premium.
Playoffs: 2 wild-card games, 1 divisional game
This is the faithful home of “Sunday Night Football” each weekend. And because everything has to be confusing, the NBC lineup opens with a Wednesday night season premiere. At least SNF has a consistent 8:20 p.m. start time.
Mike Tirico and Cris Collinsworth are in the booth, with Melissa Stark reporting from the sidelines. Carrie Underwood sings about waiting all day for Sunday night . NBC’s “Football Night in America” pregame show brings on longtime head coach Mike Tomlin. Telemundo has the telecasts in Spanish.
The network has two extra Saturday offerings for Week 17. One is exclusive to Peacock, and both matchups will be announced later in the season. The same goes for NBC’s Week 18 regular-season finale.
“Sunday Night Football” is subject to flex scheduling — games can be swapped in and out of the window twice between Weeks 5-10 and any time from Weeks 11-17. This allows executives to pick games with greater playoff implications, though it leaves the actual ticket holders in a bind.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing, or a Peacock account with the live sports plan.
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, Super Bowl LXI
The Disney networks combine to cover 17 “Monday Night Football” games. Ten of those are on both ABC and ESPN, with another seven exclusive to the latter. The oft-maligned “Monday Night Football” doubleheader is now a thing of the past.
MNF kickoffs have 8:15 p.m. starts, and their schedule flexes can happen any time in Weeks 12-17. The two Saturday ABC/ESPN matchups in Week 18 will be set as the postseason picture sharpens.
ESPN is preparing for its first Super Bowl broadcast ever on Feb. 14, 2027. It will be simulcast on ABC.
Joe Buck handles play-by-play for MNF. He’s joined by analyst Troy Aikman, plus the sideline duo of Lisa Salters and Laura Rutledge. Spanish-language airings can be found on ESPN Deportes. For 12 regular-season games and the Super Bowl, ESPN2 offers an alternate “ManningCast,” in which Eli and Peyton Manning watch the games with famous fans. Guests have ranged from Bill Belichick to Lil Wayne .
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for ABC, or an ESPN Unlimited account.
Main window: Thursday night
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game
Most weeks begin with “Thursday Night Football,” which kicks off at 8:15 p.m. Those games are behind the Prime paywall, but they’re free over the air in the participants’ home markets. Flex rules around TNF are a bit less hectic, with two allotments between Weeks 13-17.
Thursdays are called by Al Michaels and Kirk Herbstreit, with Kaylee Hartung on sideline duty. Herbstreit loves dogs ; Michaels hates vegetables . Prime has Spanish-language coverage and advanced stat broadcast options within its app. Former Jets quarterback Ryan Fitzpatrick is one of the pregame, halftime and postgame personalities.
What you’ll need to watch: Amazon Prime. TNF is also free on Twitch with a registered…

full_text:
Philadelphia Eagles running back Saquon Barkley, right, and head coach Nick Sirianni have a common interest in the 2015 self-help book "Chop Wood Carry Water." Terence Lewis / Icon Sportswire via Getty Images
PHILADELPHIA — Saquon Barkley glanced toward the 125-page, blue paperback book titled “Chop Wood Carry Water” brought to his locker in January and considered how those words helped him during a challenging season.
“Did you read it?” he asked.
He received the book as a rookie. It didn’t register with him until his 2,000-yard campaign in 2024. He used it as a resource throughout the 2025 season.
“OK, Chapter 2 is probably my favorite,” Barkley said, referring to a chapter titled “Building Your Own House.”
“I like the training under pressure one,” he added, referencing different chapters in the book that resonate with him.
Then, he found the passage he wanted.
“The danger of comparison,” said Barkley, one season after entering NFL record books. “Comparison is stealing joy. There we go.”
Seven months later, Barkley sat in a team meeting to begin the Philadelphia Eagles’ 2026 training camp. Standing in front of the room, Eagles coach Nick Sirianni shared summer reading with the team. It was the same book — Joshua Medcalf’s 2015 self-published self-help title.
“I gave this book to some of you guys, have some extra copies in there if some of you are interested in this book, ‘Chop Wood Carry Water,'” Sirianni told the players, as documented by team footage. “Really good book. It’s about how to fall in love with the process. And my favorite chapter in this book was being faithful in the small things. …Here are the highlights of this chapter: Focus on the small things, focus on the things you can control.”
Chop wood carry water pic.twitter.com/YWHHM0RwA4
— Philadelphia Eagles (@Eagles) July 30, 2026
Sirianni read an excerpt from the book to the team, focusing on the concept that the small things are “not sexy — they’re often boring.” He suggested such an approach is often “in conflict with our society.” He wanted the Eagles to focus on effort, conditioning, understanding assignments, ball security. (He even referenced “effort is free,” a motto from Jalen Hurts’ father, longtime Texas high school football coach Averion Hurts, that Sirianni now shares with his own son.) They won’t be hailed as innovative, but they are the bedrock of Sirianni’s messaging entering 2026. He used this book to crystallize it.
The Eagles posted the clip from their meeting on social media accounts. Medcalf, the author of 12 books, left a San Diego barber studio on July 29 when he was alerted to the team’s clip. (One of the messages came from Joel Embiid’s long-time trainer.) The clip went viral.
Medcalf hears from athletes and coaches who use his books as resources. Different coaches and players find varying passages in “Chop Wood Carry Water” to emphasize. Some don’t want it publicized, treating their takeaways almost like trade secrets. Others are more forthcoming about the book’s impact.
Either way, the book has become a staple in sports circles and even the business world.
Penn State coach Matt Campbell, who was Sirianni’s housemate at Mount Union, gave the book to staffers in his new program when he took the job in December . Another one of Medcalf’s books had become a mantra for one of Campbell’s teams at Iowa State and was publicized on national television. Ohio State coach Ryan Day assigned the book to his team last season . John Calipari put it in the spotlight in 2019 while coaching Kentucky’s basketball team. Kansas City Royals slugger Jac Caglianone cited it as an inspiration in preparing his standout season .
“Chop Wood Carry Water” follows a young boy’s journey to become a samurai warrior and is filled with lessons along the way. Medcalf said his central message was to find identity in who you are, not what you do — a lesson with particular relevance in an NFL meeting room. Still, he understands that each reader may take something different from the book.
So, if Sirianni finds fondness for one chapter or there’s a different concept that resonates with Barkley, Medcalf isn’t worried about whether their interpretation matches his intention. It matters that they’re finding value.
“My job is not to be judge and jury on my own stuff,” Medcalf said in a phone interview. “My job is not to worry about what people get out of it, or what they don’t get out of it. My job is to make s— and hit publish, and what they take from that is what they take from it. … I don’t start with the end user in mind and say, ‘Oh, what is it exactly that I’m trying to teach them?’ More where I come from is: What do I wish I would have known, and what do I wish I had? And I try and put that into a story form.”
So, why did Sirianni bring it to the team?
He’s always been thoughtful about what he conveys in meetings. He takes summer walks in his New Jersey neighborhood pondering the particulars of messaging. He’s sought anecdotes and examples to illustrate core principles in fresh ways. Sirianni needed an impetus to recommend a book — and then pass it around.
Sirianni said the book reinforced his belief that success has no secret formula; it comes from difficult, unglamorous work.
“Sometimes we can get caught up in the flash of whatever, but at the end of the day, tackling wins,” Sirianni said. “At the end of the day, block destruction wins. At the end of the day, toughness wins. At the end of the day, ball security and takeaway ability wins. At the end of the day, blocking wins. So, all these fundamentals that can get overlooked sometimes are what makes it happen.
“The only way to get better at those fundamentals — it’s not going to happen just because you’re talented. It’s going to happen because of the work that you put in. I can just resonate with that so much. So many of our guys on the team can resonate with that so much.”
Aaron Wellman, then the New York Giants’ strength and conditioning coach, recommended the book to Barkley when the running back came into the league in 2018. It didn’t interest Barkley much at the time. He scanned a few pages, but a psychology book was not a priority for a 21-year-old rookie at the time. Barkley finally read it after his historic 2024 season, when a more mature outlook and added life experience opened his mind to the book’s concepts. “I was like, ‘Oh s—! …Wish I read the whole thing when he gave it to me,” Barkley said.
Barkley topped 2,000 yards and won Offensive Player of the Year in 2024, while helping lead the Eagles to a win in Super Bowl LIX. It was one of the great seasons by a running back in NFL history. Then, in 2025, yards were harder to come by. His production dipped, and Barkley realized that consistency and diligence in his process must remain uncompromised.
He texted people close to him. One message he received? “Go back to chopping wood and carrying water.” He started reading the book again.
“It’s been very helpful for me, because it’s easy to stick to the process and be consistent with the work when you rush for 2,000 yards,” Barkley said in January. “And then the year doesn’t start how you wanted to start, and you don’t have all these yards that people might expect you to have, or some people didn’t expect me to have, and it shows just how important it is to set your own expectations and just focus on the things that matter and being process-driven rather than worrying about the outcome. That’s something that’s helpful to me.”
Barkley emphasized that the lessons extend beyond football. He might open a business one day. He could pursue another career post-football.
He said earlier in his career, he was more “results-driven.” The process — admittedly a buzzy word in Philadelphia — must be his north star. He wants to carry that approach into whatever awaits after retirement.
“It’s really important to me as a father,” Barkley said. “It’s something I’m happy that I was able to learn, and I want to instill that into my kids.”
More of the book…

Less than a week remains until the Seattle Seahawks begin the defense of their Super Bowl title.
