title: 6 Winners, 7 Losers From Commanders’ Initial 53-Man Roster
full_text:
The Washington Commanders' initial 53-man roster settled several positional competitions that had been ongoing since the team started its offseason program months ago. Making or missing the 53 doesn't define a winner or loser; a better measure is how much a player's standing changed over the offseason program. To make rational decisions , Washington's front office separated individual evaluations from the ugly results of the last two preseason games and looked for players who distinguished themselves during that phase. "You’re looking at the individual performances and who stood out and really separated themselves," Commanders GM Adam Peters said . Below are six players whose stock rose enough to earn jobs and seven whose paths took a different turn as their active roster spots disappeared.
OL Tanoa Togiai The undrafted rookie who was likely the biggest surprise on the initial 53-man roster was Utah guard Tanoa Togiai. At the beginning of summer, most didn't even know who he was, much less believed he'd survive roster cuts. The constantly shifting offensive line gave him opportunities for extended snaps in preseason, with Washington having the chance to evaluate nearly every single combination. Togiai is clear proof that draft status means nothing if a player performs after signing as an undrafted free agent and convinces the staff he deserves one of the nine offensive line spots. It will be interesting to see where he goes on the depth chart this season. QB Athan Kaliakmanis Athan Kaliakmanis went from a seventh-round developmental quarterback fighting Sam Hartman for reps to a player Washington wasn't willing to risk losing on waivers. His biggest jump came against Detroit, when he completed 11 of 14 passes for 162 yards and generated Washington's three longest offensive plays. Peters said Monday the preseason confirmed many of the traits the team saw when it drafted him. "He made a lot of really big-time throws in the preseason," Peters said. "And he’s not afraid to rip it." Peters then put a bow on the entire competition by saying, "Athan certainly earned that." That's about as definitive as it gets for a rookie who entered camp with no guarantees and left it with a spot on the active roster.
#Commanders QB Athan Kaliakmanis (The Greek Rifle) All-22 vs the Lions • 11 for 14 passing (79%) • 162 pass yds • 114.9 RTG • 92.4 PFF grade #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/j0tXnFAMNT
K Drew Stevens Drew Stevens had one of the cleanest paths from unknown to starter of anyone on the roster. The undrafted rookie began camp competing against Jake Moody and gradually created enough separation that Washington ended the competition before preseason was even finished . Stevens then backed up the decision by making both field goal attempts against Detroit and never gave the staff a reason to reconsider. He entered camp fighting for an NFL opportunity and left it as Washington's starting kicker. EDGE Joshua Josephs Joshua Josephs may have been the most consistent rookie riser of the entire summer. Once the pads came out, the fifth-round pick started showing the length, bend, and pass-rush traits Washington believed it was getting when it drafted him. Those flashes followed him through joint practices and into the preseason, including his fumble-recovery touchdown against Detroit. Josephs is no longer fighting just to stay on the roster. The more interesting question now is how many defensive snaps Washington can find for him during the regular season. OT D.J. Humphries D.J. Humphries didn't have months to make his case. He barely had days. Washington signed the veteran tackle late in camp after Laremy Tunsil's injury left the team searching for more reliable depth on the outside. His 101 career starts and extensive experience at left tackle gave Washington something the room was missing, and apparently the staff saw enough in a short evaluation window to keep him. Several offensive linemen spent the entire summer competing for those final spots, yet Humphries arrived late and still walked away with one. EDGE Javontae Jean-Baptiste Javontae Jean-Baptiste entered camp in a difficult position after missing most of last season and watching Washington add multiple pass rushers ahead of him. Then Josephs started surging, creating even more pressure on the former seventh-round pick. Jean-Baptiste responded by continuing to create disruptive reps and recording a sack against Detroit. Washington ultimately found room for both young edge rushers, which says plenty about how Jean-Baptiste performed when his roster spot was being challenged.
Javontae Jean-Baptiste with a great sack against the Lions in the preseason. pic.twitter.com/pcGmMnDfgm
RB Robert Henry Jr. Robert Henry Jr. went from being one of Washington's biggest preseason stories to missing the initial 53. His 12-carry, 75-yard performance against Miami , which included a touchdown, made it look like the undrafted rookie might force Washington to find room for him. Detroit changed the conversation. Henry finished with minus-3 rushing yards and fumbled a kickoff late in the game, a costly mistake for someone whose path to the roster included special teams. He showed enough this summer to make the decision interesting, but Jacory Croskey-Merritt, Rachaad White, and Kaytron Allen ultimately won the numbers game. Washington still valued Henry enough to bring him back on the practice squad, giving the rookie another opportunity to develop after losing the initial roster battle . DT Byron Cowart Byron Cowart appeared to have an opportunity once Johnny Newton's pectoral injury created more available snaps along the defensive line. Cowart showed some good things in limited work, but not enough to convince Washington he needed to be part of the initial rotation. Washington brought Cowart back on the practice squad Monday, but when an active-roster opening emerged along the defensive line, the Commanders chose to bring Shy Tuttle back instead.
Big body Byron Cowart making plays! 💪 📺 NFL Preseason on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/mqb553tJp7
OT Trent Scott Trent Scott may have fallen more than anyone on this list. Earlier in camp, his familiarity with Washington and ability to provide veteran tackle depth made him look like a reasonable bet for the 53. Then Humphries arrived, changing the numbers, and Scott followed it with a rough performance against Baltimore that included a holding penalty and surrendered pressure. The timing could not have been worse. A player who once looked like one of Washington's safer depth options ultimately watched a veteran signed late in camp take the spot. Scott did return on the practice squad, but that doesn't change the result of the competition: Humphries got the active-roster spot while Scott ended up on the practice squad. WR Van Jefferson Van Jefferson entered camp with the benefit of NFL experience, but Washington's receiver room eventually became too crowded for experience alone to win him a job. Terry McLaurin and Stefon Diggs were never in question, while younger players such as Antonio Williams, Luke McCaffrey, Treylon Burks, and Jaylin Lane gave Washington either more upside or clearer roles. Jefferson was dependable, but there wasn't enough separating him from the younger options to justify another active roster spot. LB Ale Kaho Ale Kaho did just about everything he could in the preseason finale, leading Washington with seven tackles against Baltimore. Unfortunately for him, one strong final performance couldn't completely overcome the numbers at linebacker. Frankie Luvu, Sonny Styles, and Leo Chenal already had major roles, while Washington also had younger players competing for backup and special teams work. Kaho gave the staff something to think about right up until the end, but sometimes the roster math is already working against you. Washington brought Kaho back on the practice squad, keeping him available as a linebacker and special-teams depth option despite losing the initial 53-man…

title: Adam Peters Doubles Down on Washington's Plan at Center After Roster Cuts — Commanders Daily
full_text:
With Nick Allegretti missing most of the summer with a calf injury , the center position was easily one of the Washington Commanders' biggest unresolved questions throughout training camp. While the team evaluated several options, after final roster cuts , the center position remains the same: Allegretti is back at practice as the team’s preferred option, rookie Matt Gulbin is on the 53-man roster , and Julian Good-Jones is back on the practice squad. During his co-press conference with head coach Dan Quinn, Adam Peters doubled down on his confidence in Allegretti. The team abruptly released former center Tyler Biadasz before free agency, who then signed a new deal with the Los Angeles Chargers a few days later. When The Athletic’s Nicki Jhabvala asked Peters about the offseason decision-making at center, he wasn't interested in rehashing the team’s pursuit of other options: "Yeah, I mean, that's something we've already covered a little bit, I think, Nikki, in terms of I don't want to go back and talk about Tyler and all that. But certainly we feel very confident in Nick, and we have," Peters said . "And that's where we went into this offseason feeling that Nick could be our starter, and still do feel that way. And who we went for and who we did or didn't get, I don't think we want to get into rewriting history, talking about six months ago. But those are the guys that we're really excited to see go play here in a couple Sundays." While Washington's confidence in Allegretti hasn't changed , his lack of training camp work still leaves a legitimate question about how quickly the group can come together. Quinn also chimed in, saying Washington is still working through the center position while welcoming Allegretti back to practice. Peters added that Allegretti doesn't need a large volume of reps from a mental standpoint. He also praised Gulbin's development, while Quinn specifically praised the rookie's strength, football intelligence, and ability to avoid repeating mistakes. Ultimately, this summer now seems more about determining Washington's contingency plans rather than finding a suitable replacement center. While the front office owning the plan at center is great optics, Allegretti still needs to hold up his part of the plan physically.
